editions.title: Microsoft quits Nscale site as AI trade wobbles and iPhone Duo supply strains
editions.intro:
The biggest story is a reported setback for Nscale, the British AI cloud startup. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has pulled out of a deal to anchor Nscale's first UK data centre in Loughton, Essex, weeks before Nscale's planned IPO of up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, and Microsoft has not commented. The report lands as investors grow wary of neocloud firms, and CoreWeave shares were marked down in coverage of the story.

The wider backdrop is a deepening selloff in US tech shares. Bloomberg reports that this is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI "picks and shovels" suppliers, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The FT also argues that America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical constraints. Against that, SemiAnalysis says more than 300 local data-centre moratoriums have delayed only a few projects so far. Meta's earnings, previewed by the FT as a test of confidence in AI spending, are the next major read-across.

Apple dominated the rest of the day's flow. The iPhone Duo, its first foldable, is reportedly sold out into January, with staff told walk-in buyers are unlikely to get stock on launch day, and Gurman calls the staggered pre-order rollout a "major mistake". Apple's EU energy label put the device's battery at 4,883 mAh. Rumours also point to a touchscreen MacBook and a HomeView smart display with a robotic arm, with a possible retail refresh on 6 November. Most of these remain unconfirmed.

top_stories.summary: Apple Store staff reportedly told customers without pre-orders to expect no launch-day stock. Apple says demand is extraordinary, and shipping estimates have slipped to around late January in most countries.

editions.title: Microsoft Walks Away From Nscale Site as Neocloud Nerves Grow
editions.intro:
The biggest story of the day is Microsoft's reported withdrawal from an anchor deal for Nscale's first British data centre in Loughton, Essex. The Telegraph says Microsoft has pulled out weeks before the AI cloud startup's planned IPO, which is reported to seek up to $3bn. Nscale says it remains committed to the site and that its Microsoft relationship is strong, while Microsoft has not commented. Grid connection delays at the site were also reported, and the story is being read as a sign of wider caution toward neocloud firms.

That caution fed into a broader theme of AI-trade nerves. Bloomberg reports that a deepening selloff in US tech shares is exposing weak spots in Asia's AI supply chain, with rising financing costs threatening data-centre and hardware spending. The Financial Times, meanwhile, argues America's roughly $10tn AI infrastructure build-out is running into physical limits of power, equipment and money. Investors will look to Meta's earnings next, which the FT frames as a test of whether confidence in the AI spending boom can be restored.

Elsewhere, Ericsson beat expectations with third-quarter adjusted EBITA of SEK 10.1bn against a consensus of SEK 7.93bn, and its shares rose as much as 11% in Stockholm. On the chip front, a single unverified report says Nvidia wants Samsung, Micron and SK hynix to build custom HBM base dies on TSMC's 3nm process, while a separate rumour suggests China could let major firms buy H200 chips under tight caps. Both remain unconfirmed.

editions.title: Nvidia RTX 5090 Row, TSMC Profit Record and Starlink Limits Dominate
editions.intro: TSMC posted a record quarterly profit, with demand for AI chips still far outstripping supply, but it signalled caution on 2027. Meanwhile, the AI trade showed strain: Asian chip suppliers were exposed to a US tech selloff, and reports that OpenAI's revenue trails expectations added to nerves. Ukraine's dispute with SpaceX over Starlink speed limits escalated, with Zelenskyy calling the restrictions deliberate. Apple's iPhone Duo faced shortages and Apple's chief executive called memory supply a crisis.

top_stories.title: TSMC records sixth straight record profit, cautious on 2027
top_stories.summary: TSMC reported record third-quarter net profit of NT$763.1bn, up 69%, with revenue up 51%. It guided to about 44% dollar revenue growth in 2026, but chairman C.C. Wei warned that price-sensitive consumer markets are under pressure and that the company is being prudent about 2027.

top_stories.title: Starshield speed limits cut Ukrainian interceptor drones
top_stories.summary: Speed limits on SpaceX's Starshield network reportedly cut links for interceptor drones above about 161 km/h, forcing Ukrainian units to cancel missions. Reports suggest the order came from the White House or was discussed by Musk and Trump, but these claims are unverified.

top_stories.title: Apple's Ternus calls memory shortage a crisis
top_stories.summary: Apple's chief executive told TIME that memory chip constraints are a crisis and all options should be considered. The comments follow a report that Apple tested memory chips from a Chinese firm, which prompted US warnings against them.

top_stories.title: Microsoft plans multi-gigawatt Maia 300 rollout
top_stories.summary: Microsoft plans to scale its Maia accelerators to multi-gigawatt deployments from 2027, with Maia 300 as its primary inference system. Analysts expect Maia to be only about 10% of its AI chip spend by early 2027, so Nvidia's position is not yet under threat.

top_stories.title: Intel confirms Razor Lake-AX timing and 700 TOPS target
top_stories.summary: Intel SVP Cho Min-sung confirmed Nova Lake for 2027 and Razor Lake-AX for 2028, the latter targeting 700 TOPS of AI compute. The aim is premium devices and physical AI.

top_stories.title: Tesla shows fan-powered Roadster, production 2028
top_stories.summary: Tesla demonstrated its next-generation Roadster using powered fans and a retractable rear wing for downforce. Musk said production begins in 2028, with reservations open at $50,000 for the base model and $250,000 for the Thrust trim.

rumour_watch.note: A reported $20bn revenue shortfall at OpenAI, relayed without a named source. Plausible given the market backdrop, but it is an internal figure and OpenAI has not confirmed it.
Nvidia's Jeff Fisher reportedly denied the RTX 5090 is discontinued, citing tight supply. Credible on the record, but retailer listings at inflated prices suggest supply is genuinely thin.
Reported FTC demands aimed at OpenAI and Anthropic. Only a feed summary, and the story stresses it is not a finding of wrongdoing, so treat as unconfirmed.
DeepSeek says its new Flash model beats larger rivals on agentic tasks. Weights are public, but independent benchmarks are still pending.

Anduril opens a $1.3bn employee tender at a $90bn valuation, up from $61bn in May.
Berkshire Hathaway buys a further $330m of Bending Spoons shares, lifting its stake to about 4%.
Netflix names Peter Rice chief content officer as Bela Bajaria leaves, a day after a 6% staff cut.
Meta removes contested scraping language from its commercial terms after criticism from publishers and experts.

Finance.title: AI selloff spreads to Asia as rates and oil bite
Finance.notification: Chip stocks suffer their longest rout since 2008 as rising borrowing costs threaten AI spending.
Finance.summary:
The dominant theme is a sharp reversal in AI-linked equities. US chip stocks had an eight-session rout, the longest since 2008, and the Philadelphia semiconductor index fell about 16 percent. The selloff has spread to Asia's AI supply chain, with a Goldman Sachs basket of regional hardware stocks down 11 percent last week. Investors fear that rising borrowing costs could curb the data-centre spending that has powered the rally, and analysts warn that financing strain at hyperscalers and neoclouds such as CoreWeave could reduce orders for TSMC, Samsung and SK Hynix. Some investors argue demand remains strong.

The wider market backdrop is nervous. Wall Street's weekly wrap showed the Nasdaq down 4.48 percent and the S&P 500 down 1.95 percent, while September CPI rose 3.7 percent year on year and the VIX jumped above 21. Ten-year Treasury yields have climbed above 5 percent, and oil has risen above $100 a barrel, with one report citing $110. Barclays warns that markets and the economy now lean heavily on AI earnings, while UBS argues the S&P 500 can absorb further Fed hikes.

Elsewhere, pressure is building in other markets. French bond yields are expected to rise after nationwide violent protests, with economists warning of a sell-off in French debt, and Indonesian equities had their worst day since 1998 after an MSCI downgrade warning. Israel's and Russia-linked energy stories add to geopolitical risk, with Iranian mine attacks in the Strait of Hormuz pushing oil higher.

points.text: French bond yields seen rising after violent protests; economists warn of a possible jump of up to 0.1 points.
Indonesian stocks suffered their steepest one-day fall since 1998 after MSCI warned it could downgrade the market.
Weekly wrap: Nasdaq down 4.48 percent, S&P 500 down 1.95 percent, with Apple passing a $5 trillion market value.
UBS says the S&P 500 can withstand Fed hikes and raised its year-end 10-year yield forecast to 4.9 percent.
Barclays warns that markets and the economy now lean heavily on AI earnings, with bond yields at multi-decade highs.
Michael Burry warns of a 2000-style reckoning, noting 55 percent of S&P 500 stocks are in bear markets.

World.title: France riots spread as Europe's cost-of-living anger grows
World.notification: Paris riots, over 2,000 arrests and a crisis in Macron's government: what the unrest means for markets.
World.summary:
Student-led protests in France have turned into the worst unrest in years, with burnt cars, looted shops and public buildings set alight in Paris, Limoges and elsewhere. Reported arrests run above 2,000, and the government has held crisis talks after what one outlet called a "colossal failure of the state". Opposition politicians from left and right want the interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, to resign. The unrest is linked to cost-of-living and school funding grievances, and similar housing-cost protests have spread to Italy, Portugal, Spain and Albania.

Markets reacted mainly through France. The CAC 40 is lower, and Paris-listed names such as LVMH were also down. Traders' unions say more than 1,500 businesses were ransacked. Political risk in the eurozone's second-largest economy is the key concern, and the euro was softer against the dollar in some reports.

Elsewhere, the Russia-Ukraine energy war is escalating after a short-lived energy ceasefire collapsed. Ukrainian drones hit St Petersburg oil facilities, and oil prices rose. Washington has paused a sweeping Russia sanctions package for 60 days, a move criticised across both US parties. Gulf states backed Saudi Arabia after Houthi attacks, while Israel's election on 27 October and settler violence in the West Bank continue to draw attention.

points.text: Ministers face calls to resign over the French unrest, with more than 1,500 businesses reported ransacked.
Russia and Ukraine resumed strikes on energy sites after Trump's energy ceasefire quickly broke down.

GCC states condemned Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia and backed its right to self-defence; oil prices rose.
Taiwan says it drove away 16 Chinese vessels in what it calls hybrid warfare around the main island and Pratas.
Protests drew over half a million people in France, and Macron faces criticism over a Celine Dion concert visit.

Tech.title: Nscale setback and AI spending doubts weigh on tech
Tech.notification: Microsoft reportedly quits Nscale's Essex data centre weeks before its New York IPO.
Tech.summary:
The biggest story in tech today is the reported setback for Nscale, the British AI infrastructure firm. The Telegraph reports that Microsoft has ended its agreement to anchor Nscale's Loughton data centre in Essex, where grid power was reportedly not expected until the 2030s. Nscale says it remains committed to the site, is exploring other power supplies and that its Microsoft relationship is strong. The timing is awkward, as the company has filed for a New York listing under the ticker NSCL, and Microsoft and Anthropic account for about 85% of its contracts.

The Nscale news sits within a wider mood of caution about AI spending. Bloomberg reports a deepening selloff in US tech shares that is exposing weakness in Asia's chip supply chain, and a Bloomberg-cited report says Google's flagship Gemini 3.5 Pro is months behind schedule, with Alphabet shares falling about 4.5% in a session. Separately, reports say OpenAI's $500 billion Stargate project has hit obstacles and that its planned AI infrastructure spending has been scaled back to $600 billion through 2030, prompting a sceptical response from Elon Musk.

Elsewhere, Apple dominates the consumer news, with its foldable iPhone Duo facing supply-constrained pre-orders and shipping dates slipping into 2027 for some models. Several Apple product reports, including a touchscreen MacBook and a robotic HomeView, remain unconfirmed rumours. Meanwhile, Anthropic is pushing for norms on AI agents and an external safety evaluator, and Character.AI's assets are heading to Disney.

Fashion.title: Creative churn hits Calvin Klein and McQueen
Fashion.notification: Seán McGirr is leaving Alexander McQueen, and Calvin Klein has lost Veronica Leoni. Who fills the seats?
Fashion.summary:
The clearest story today is a wave of creative leadership change. Seán McGirr is leaving Alexander McQueen after three years, with his Spring/Summer 2027 London show as his final collection. He succeeded Sarah Burton, who moved to Givenchy, and his tenure brought the Kering-owned house back to London with a younger, club-influenced approach that drew mixed reviews. Separately, Vogue Scandinavia reports that Veronica Leoni is departing Calvin Klein after four seasons, though the feed gives no detail on her role or successor. A New York Times piece asks who should fill the open roles at both labels, underlining how many top seats are now vacant.

The business backdrop looks uneasy. The Business of Fashion describes a difficult period for luxury, with weak numbers and empty chairs, while another BoF item questions whether the United States can keep supporting luxury demand. In China, Chanel is preparing its first Wuhan store at SKP, sitting on a pedestrian promenade alongside Louis Vuitton and Cartier, as luxury brands there close weak stores and test new regional markets. Hublot has also hired former Audemars Piguet chief François-Henri Bennahmias as a consultant.

Elsewhere, Cartier unveiled the second chapter of its high jewellery collection in Kyoto, with the Stellara necklace the highlight, and Vacheron Constantin and Phillips named 34 finalists for a historic watch competition. Victoria's Secret's Pink takes the show's halftime slot, and Rosie Huntington-Whiteley returns to the runway after 16 years.
